findings.headline: Sickness absence stood at 3.19 days lost per FTE in Q2 2026/27, up from 2.51 days in Q1 2026/27 and 2.16 days in Q2 2025/26, with 42.52 FTE vacancies being recruited.
findings.detail: The paper reports stress and depression as the highest cause of both short-term and long-term absence in the quarter. Turnover was 2.10%, lower than the 3.02% in Q1, and the paper records 66.30 FTE vacancies at the end of Q2.
findings.matters: Absence and vacancy levels drive the cost of delivering services and the overtime and agency spend that follows, which finance directors compare across councils.
findings.figures: 3.19 days lost per FTE; 2.51 days in Q1 2026/27; 2.16 days in Q2 2025/26; 42.52 FTE vacancies being recruited; 66.30 FTE vacancies; 2.10% turnover (3.02% in Q1)
findings.quote: During quarter 2 2026/27 the total sickness levels for the council stood at 3.19 days lost per FTE.

findings.headline: The Housing Ombudsman determined one complaint in Q2 2026/27, finding maladministration in the landlord’s handling of reports from the resident, with 148 formal complaints recorded for the Housing directorate.
findings.detail: The paper says the Ombudsman found the council failed to properly address the resident's concerns or follow up on solutions it agreed to consider, and delayed escalating the stage 2 request. Housing received 148 formal complaints in the quarter, an increase of 43 on Q1, and 62% of those were upheld.
findings.matters: A Housing Ombudsman maladministration finding is a public regulatory outcome for a social landlord, and a rise in complaints and upheld rates is the kind of signal lenders to social housing look for.
findings.figures: 1 Housing Ombudsman complaint decided; 148 DHI complaints (up 43); 223 total formal complaints; 125 (56%) upheld in Q2; 92 (62%) DHI upheld
findings.quote: with findings of maladministration in the landlord’s handling of reports from the resident

findings.headline: The UKSPF 2025/26 programme completed in Q2 2026/27 with 100% of spend delivered and all outputs achieved across 10 projects.
findings.detail: The paper says the programme was contracted from June 2025 to September 2026. An evaluation of the whole UKSPF programme is underway and will go to a future committee, and the paper asks for measures DMD 3 and DMD 4 to be removed from quarterly reporting.
findings.matters: Shared Prosperity Fund programmes are closing across councils, and a finance officer checking grant close-out would want to know spend and outputs were fully delivered.
findings.figures: 100% spend (Q1 64%); 100% on target (Q1 91%); 10 projects; June 2025 to September 2026
findings.quote: The UKSPF 2025/26 has now completed, with 100% of the percentage spend delivered, with all outputs achieved.

findings.headline: The Town Deal programme, with 14 projects, now has an extension to March 2027, with 87% of spend and 93% of projects on target in Q2 2026/27.
findings.detail: The paper says all remaining funds have been reallocated and signed off by government and the Board. Five projects are financially complete, eight are on target and one is within programme.
findings.matters: A government-funded capital programme extended past its original end date, with spend and milestones reported, is a deadline and delivery risk other councils running Towns Fund schemes will track.
findings.figures: 14 projects; 87% spend (Q1 83%); 93% on target (Q1 75%); March 2027; 5 financially complete; 8 on target; 1 within programme
findings.quote: The programme now has an extension to March 2027.

findings.headline: Average interest rate on external borrowing was 3.4% in Q2 2026/27, unchanged from Q1 and against a 3.50% high target, while the average return on investments was 3.89%.
findings.detail: The paper says there was no material change in borrowing costs in Q1. The reduction in investment return from 3.98% to 3.89% is attributed to the maturity of fixed-term investments in Q1, and the measure sits below the 4.00% high target.
findings.matters: Borrowing cost and investment return together set the net cost of the council's treasury position, which lenders and finance directors compare across councils.
findings.figures: 3.4% (Q1 and Q2); 3.50% high target; 3.89% investment return; 3.98% in Q1; 4.00% high target
findings.quote: No material change in the average interest paid on borrowing in Q1.

findings.headline: Sessional car parking income reached 101.96% of budget requirement in Q2 2026/27, with income of £1,956,412.24 against a budget of £1,918,755.00.
findings.detail: The paper says income exceeded budget in all three months of the quarter, though the margin was smaller than in recent quarters, which it attributes to challenging circumstances. It states the service is on track to meet the yearly target.
findings.matters: Car parking is a discretionary income line that councils budget tightly, and this shows a fee-income stream running ahead of budget at mid-year.
findings.quote: Income for the quarter was £1,956,412.24 against a budget of £1,918,755.00.

findings.headline: Business Rates in-year collection for Lincoln was 58.33% at the end of Q2 2026/27, 1.05% lower than at the same point in 2025/26.
findings.detail: The paper says the position improved significantly during the quarter, from more than 4% below the previous year at the end of August. It attributes delays to instalment plans being pushed later after amended bills could not be sent out promptly.
findings.matters: Business Rates collection drives the Collection Fund and retained-rates position, so a year-on-year shortfall at mid-year is relevant to the budget forecast.
findings.figures: 58.33%; 1.05% lower than Q2 2025/26; more than 4% below at end of August; 50.00% low target; 48.00% high target
findings.quote: The collection rate at the end of Q2 2026/27 is 1.05% lower than at the same point in 2025/26.

findings.headline: In-year Council Tax collection for Lincoln was 50.03% at the end of Q2 2026/27, an increase of 0.4% on 2025/26 and below the 51.50% high target.
findings.detail: The paper describes collection as challenging. Its status for the measure is amber, and it reports no separate figure for the year-on-year movement beyond the 0.4% increase.
findings.matters: Council Tax in-year collection feeds the council's cash flow and its Collection Fund position, which finance directors and lenders track closely.
findings.quote: The Council Tax in year collection figure delivered a small increase of 0.4% when compared to 2025/26.

findings.headline: Rent collected as a proportion of rent owed reached 98.37% in Q2 2026/27, above the 97.50% target and up from 97.89% in Q1.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the result to income recovery activity and early intervention with tenants facing financial difficulty. Current tenant arrears rose from 3.49% in Q1 to 3.64% in Q2 but remain below the 4.00% low target.
findings.matters: Rent collection is the main cash inflow for the HRA, and the arrears trend shows whether the collection rate is holding as cost-of-living pressure continues.
findings.figures: 98.37%; 97.50% target; 97.89% in Q1; current tenant arrears 3.64% (3.49% in Q1); 4.00% target
findings.quote: Rent collection performance remains strong at 98.37% for Q2, exceeding the target of 97.50%

findings.headline: Average re-let time for all dwellings was 68.43 calendar days in Q2 2026/27, against a high target of 42.00 days, as approximately 75% of voids now need major works.
findings.detail: The paper says the shift from minor to major works has increased labour demand and extended turnaround. Standard void turnaround was 59.92 days and major works void turnaround was 82.00 days. Fixed-term operatives recruited for the stock condition programme have been redeployed to voids, and more major works voids are being kept in-house to reduce subcontractor costs.
findings.matters: A move to major-works voids raises the capital cost per re-let and extends rent loss, which affects both HRA spend and income.
findings.figures: 68.43 days; 42.00 days high target; 59.92 days standard; 82.00 days major works; approximately 75%
findings.quote: approximately 75% of current voids now require major works, compared to around 25% requiring minor works.

findings.headline: Rent lost through dwellings being vacant was 1.82% in Q2 2026/27, down from 1.90% in Q1 and above the 1.00% target.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the figure to 29 miscellaneous properties and 10 decant units that are not available for re-let but remain in the rent loss figures. It states that removing live miscellaneous voids and decants would give approximately 1.22% for the quarter.
findings.matters: Rent loss on vacant HRA stock is direct lost income, and the paper quantifies how much of it sits in decant and miscellaneous units rather than routine voids.
findings.figures: 1.82%; 1.90%; target 1.00%; 29 miscellaneous properties; 10 decant units; approximately 1.22%
findings.quote: Rent loss through dwellings being vacant is 1.82% at the end of Q2, an improvement from 1.90% in Q1, although it remains above the 1.00% target.

findings.headline: Council properties not meeting the Decent Homes standard fell 17.4% to 413 in Q2 2026/27, which is 5.34% of council properties against a 1.00% high target.
findings.detail: The paper says 46 additional non-compliant properties were identified against Q1 through the enhanced stock condition programme, which masks progress. All three High Rise Buildings are in feasibility studies, and 136 flats at Trent View and Jarvis House do not meet the standard for windows and/or doors.
findings.matters: A stock investment backlog and high-rise remediation are capital and HRA exposures that a lender or finance director would need to see sized against the investment plan.
findings.figures: 5.34%; 413 properties; 17.4%; 46 additional properties; 136 flats; high target 1.00%
findings.quote: properties that do not meet the standard have decreased by 17.4% to 413 properties.

findings.headline: Draft MTFS 2027-2032 due to be presented to the Executive on 19th January 2027, with base budget adjustments required.
findings.detail: The paper says the council continues to face ongoing pressures from inflation, service demand and income, and that the MTFS 2027-2032 will need base budget adjustments to address them. The paper also says the risk assessment is continually reviewed in the MTFS.
findings.matters: The date and the statement that base budgets must be adjusted set the timetable against which a finance director would judge whether the council can close its structural gap.
findings.figures: Draft MTFS 2027-2032 due 19th January 2027; prudent minimum General Fund balances £1.5m-£2m, HRA £1m-£1.5m
findings.quote: Development of the MTFS 2027-2032 is currently in progress and will require the adjustment of base budgets in order to address the financial challenges being faced.

findings.headline: Total earmarked reserves forecast to fall from £12,782k at 1 April 2026 to £9,443k at 31 March 2027.
findings.detail: The paper shows General Fund earmarked reserves falling from £7,671k to £6,320k and HRA earmarked reserves falling from £5,111k to £3,123k over the year. The paper says a number of the reserves are budgeted for use over the MTFS period.
findings.matters: A fall of £3,339k in total earmarked reserves in one year, across both funds, is a drawdown a finance director at another council would compare against their own reserve trajectory.
findings.figures: Total earmarked reserves £12,782k opening, £9,443k forecast closing; General Fund £7,671k to £6,320k; HRA £5,111k to £3,123k

findings.headline: Housing Investment Programme cut by £5.704m to £22.860m at Q2, with £7.617m spent by 30 September, 33.32% of the revised programme.
findings.detail: The paper says the Jasmin Green new build scheme was reprofiled by £4,226k into 2027/28 and the environmental works budget by £1,200k. The New Build Programme spend is 41.53% of its revised budget, against 33.32% for the whole programme.
findings.matters: Reprofiling a major new-build scheme into later years alongside a lower HRA contribution to the MRR shows the investment programme being slowed, which affects the HRA's long-term capital capacity.
findings.figures: HIP revised budget £22.860m (opening £28.564m, change £5,704k); Jasmin Green reprofile £4,226k; spend £7.617m, 33.32%; a further £0.919m spent to end October
findings.quote: The overall expenditure on the Housing Investment Programme at the end of Q2 was £7.617m, which is 33.32% of the 2026/27 revised programme

findings.headline: Charterholme Phase 1c has not started on site, and General Investment Programme council schemes have spent £4.228m, 25.83% of the revised programme at Q2.
findings.detail: The paper says the General Investment Programme was cut by £8,478k at Q2, from £25.944m to £17.466m, with the largest reprofile being £5,540k on the Charterholme Phase 1c Spine Road into 2027/28. The paper states physical works on Charterholme Phase 1C have not started, with the scheme still in planning and technical design.
findings.matters: A £5.54m spine road reprofile out of the current year and works not yet on site is a signal of delivery timing on a major scheme, which a lender or peer council with similar development would want to track.
findings.figures: GIP revised budget £17.466m (opening £25.944m, change £8,478k); Charterholme Phase 1c Spine Road reprofile (£5,540k) into 2027/28; council schemes spend £4.228m, 25.83% of revised programme
findings.quote: There is a large budget for Charterholme Phase 1C for which physical works have not yet started on site, with work currently in planning and technical design stages, with minimal spend so far.

findings.headline: General Fund forecast underspend of £64,335, leaving general balances at £2,593,298 against a prudent minimum of c.£1.5m-£2m.
findings.detail: The paper reports this as a forecast underspend at Q2, but section 9 says the General Fund is forecasting a budget shortfall for 2026/27 and that the additional use of general balances may be needed. Forecast outturn is subject to further change due to service demands and income uncertainty.
findings.matters: The General Fund is reported as in underspend at Q2 while the same paper says a budget shortfall is forecast, so the position depends on which measure a reader uses; a finance director would want both figures reconciled.
findings.figures: Forecast underspend £64,335; forecast general balances £2,593,298 (opening £2,528,963); prudent minimum c.£1.5-£2m; Q2 year-end deficit/(surplus) (64)k
findings.quote: The General Fund Summary is currently projecting a forecast underspend of £64,335

findings.headline: Car parking forecast to produce a net surplus of £281k, including £192k of one-off business rates transitional relief on Central car park.
findings.detail: The paper says car parking continues to produce a surplus even after budgets were rebased to last year's activity. It also says the Council received a one-off transitional relief on the business rates increase from the 2026 revaluation, which was not known when the MTFS was approved, and is treated as non-recurrent. Part of the saving is earmarked for repairs and revenue contributions to capital.
findings.matters: A non-recurrent business rates relief helping to cover this year's position is one a finance director would need to separate from recurring income when setting the next MTFS.
findings.figures: Net car parking surplus £281k; one-off NNDR transitional relief £192k; season ticket and pay and display income increase £215,460
findings.quote: In addition to this the Council has also received a one-off transitional relief against this years budgeted increase in business rates following the Valuation Offices 2026 revaluation list

findings.headline: New leisure provider forecasts a surplus of £156,710 this year, proposed to be paid into a Leisure Sinking Fund reserve.
findings.detail: The paper says the surplus was anticipated in the original contract bid but was not in the budget, which was set at a balanced position to be prudent. The surplus is proposed to replenish a sinking fund reserve used for remobilisation costs last year.
findings.matters: A contract surplus coming in above a prudent budget and being used to rebuild a reserve shows a leisure contract performing ahead of the council's own budget assumptions.
findings.figures: Leisure centre surplus £156,710 (£'000 table: 157); contribution to Leisure Sinking Fund reserve £156,710
findings.quote: As a result, this surplus is proposed to be contributed back into a Leisure Sinking Fund reserve to replenish some of the funding utilised last financial year as part of the remobilisation costs.

findings.headline: Housing Repairs Service sub-contractor spend forecast at £1,191,320 above budget, with overhead not recovered on sub-contractor work.
findings.detail: The paper says the HRS is relying more on sub-contractors to resource voids and the rise in regulatory works. The paper states that sub-contractors cost more than the in-house workforce, and that subcontractor costs are not reflected in the hourly rate, so the HRA under-recovers full costs. The management of change review is looking at this.
findings.matters: A repairs service paying a premium for sub-contract labour that is not recovered in its rates shows a cost pattern that other councils running in-house repair services would recognise.
findings.figures: Sub-contractors forecast variance £1,191,320 (£'000 table: 1,191) against revised budget £2,194k; Direct Materials variance £321,540; HRS forecast surplus £2,667 repatriated to HRA
findings.quote: In addition, as the increased subcontractor costs are not reflected in the service hourly rate and overhead recovery is not recouped on sub-contractors this results in an under recovery of full costs from the HRA.

findings.headline: Stock condition survey HHSRS works forecast to be entirely offset by the earmarked Repairs reserve, with Damp and Mould costs partly offset by the same reserve.
findings.detail: The paper says the stock condition surveys required under new regulations are expected to finish this year and have identified more HHSRS and damp and mould work than budgeted. The HHSRS cost is fully covered by a repairs reserve set aside for this, and the Damp and Mould cost is partly covered by the same reserve, with the balance met by the MRR reduction. The paper also notes that ongoing work will be needed after remedial work.
findings.matters: A reserve set aside in advance is being drawn to meet regulatory works uncovered by surveys, which shows the reserve doing the job it was created for and leaves no balance behind for the same purpose.
findings.figures: £998,520 drawdown from the Repairs Account reserve; HHSRS repairs £404k and Damp & Mould £550k (total £953,670 increase in HRS repairs); Repairs Account reserve £999k opening, £0 closing
findings.quote: the forecast cost of which is being entirely offset by an earmarked Repairs reserve, previously set aside for this.

findings.headline: HRA forecast to require a significant reduction in the voluntary Major Repairs Reserve contribution to keep balances at the £1m prudent minimum.
findings.detail: The paper says the HRA is forecast to overspend once the significant variations are included, which would take general balances below the prudent minimum. The voluntary contribution to the Major Repairs Reserve is being cut to hold balances at £1m, and the paper says this reduces the flexibility the reserve gives for repairs fluctuations and the amount available to support the Housing Investment Programme.
findings.matters: A HRA using its voluntary reserve contribution to protect balances reduces the funding available for future investment in homes, which affects the capital programme and the long-term business plan.
findings.figures: Reduction in MRR voluntary contribution £194,780 (to maintain £1m prudent HRA working balance) and £426,100 (to offset responsive works and HHSRS/Damp and Mould recharges); forecast HRA balances £1,000,572 at 31/03/27
findings.quote: In order to ensure balances are kept at the prudent minimum, a significant reduction in the voluntary contribution to the Major Repair Reserve will be required.

findings.headline: Crematorium income shortfall of £221,340 forecast for 2026/27, wholly offset by a drawdown from the Income Volatility reserve.
findings.detail: The paper says crematorium income remains below budget, as in the last two financial years, but has stabilised and is slightly above the same period last year. The Council introduced its own direct cremation service in early 2026, which the paper describes as popular, but says the extra income is still insufficient to meet the deficit. Work is being considered on memorial services income and a longer-term strategic review.
findings.matters: A council is funding a recurring service shortfall from a volatility reserve while it looks for new income, which a lender or peer would want to track against the reserve's balance.
findings.figures: £221,340 crematorium shortfall; net crematorium deficit £184.3k; Income Volatility reserve drawdown £221,000 (£'000 table: 221); Income Volatility reserve opening balance £570k, forecast £350k
findings.quote: The shortfall in income this year is being wholly offset by a drawdown from the Income Volatility reserve.

findings.matters: A change in contract standards and measures alters how the council can judge contractor performance and value for money, which is relevant to any council with similar outsourced services.

findings.matters: Benefit processing backlogs affect the timing of benefit payments and the accuracy of council tax income, and the figure is reported as at Q1, not Q2.

findings.headline: The percentage of complaints responded to within the service standard rose to 90% in Q2 2026/27, with a year-to-date figure of 87%.
findings.detail: Of the 223 complaints dealt with in the quarter, 22 were responded to outside the target times. The report records 30 compliments in the quarter across all services.
findings.matters: On-time complaint response is a measure of administrative capacity, and an improvement from the year-to-date figure shows the trend moving towards the service standard.

findings.detail: The Ombudsman found the council failed to properly address the resident's concerns or follow up on solutions it had agreed to consider, and delayed escalating a stage 2 request. No Local Government Ombudsman complaints were decided in the quarter.

findings.detail: The report states that 14 employees left in Q2. Vacancies exclude any posts with less than 37 hours per week. The 42.52 FTE being recruited are at different stages of the recruitment process.
findings.matters: Vacancy levels and turnover determine staffing cost and service capacity, and a council carrying 66.30 FTE of vacancies may be underspending its pay budget while relying on agency or interim cover.

findings.detail: The report says the highest number of days lost to both short-term and long-term absence was attributed to stress and depression. Sickness is reported as having increased on both the previous quarter and the same quarter last year.
findings.matters: Rising sickness absence increases the cost of cover and reduces capacity in services, and a finance director will want to track it against workforce budgets.
findings.quote: the total sickness levels for the Council stood at 3.19 days lost per FTE.

findings.matters: A shift in void works from minor to major raises the per-unit cost of turning around empty homes, which affects the capital programme and the HRA budget.
findings.figures: Approximately 75% of voids require major works; around 25% require minor works

findings.detail: The report attributes the continued gap to a small number of long-term decant and potential disposal properties in the voids system. Weekly void review meetings have been introduced to reduce delays.
findings.matters: Rent loss from voids is a direct reduction in HRA income, and the report links it to specific long-term properties that will not return to rent.

findings.matters: A finance director comparing service delivery across councils can use the share of targeted measures on track as a basic indicator of how services are performing against their own targets.

findings.matters: Short-term renewals and the expected timing of further borrowing show the council's refinancing pressure, which lenders and peer finance teams watch closely.

findings.headline: The Chief Finance Officer reports that no difficulties are envisaged for the current or future years.

findings.quote: The Chief Finance Officer reports that no difficulties are envisaged for the current or future years.

findings.matters: Compliance with approved limits is a basic governance test that a finance director, auditor or lender checks first in a mid-year treasury report.
findings.quote: Officers can confirm that the approved limits within the Annual Treasury Management Strategy were not breached during the quarter ended 30th September 2026.

findings.headline: The net income ratio for commercial and service investments is below the budget-setting expectation, partly because of the number of property voids currently held.
findings.detail: The paper notes the ratio is slightly reduced from expectations at budget setting. It attributes part of the shortfall to property voids.

findings.detail: The HRA forecast shows an underspend of £244k, but this is only achieved by drawing down the Repairs Account reserve (£999k) and cutting the Major Repairs Reserve contribution (£722k). findings.detail: HRS is experiencing £912k variance in sub-contractor spend as it responds to increased workload from stock condition surveys. The council acknowledges this in a management of change review but has no resolution yet.
findings.matters: Unrecovered sub-contractor costs represent a hidden subsidy flowing from the HRA and indicate service capacity problems that cannot be solved within the existing cost model.
findings.figures: £912k sub-contractor cost variance in Q1
findings.quote: In order to try and resource the required works and meet service demands in voids and other areas, there is an increased reliance on the use of sub-contractors. The cost of using subcontractors is however more expensive than the HRS's own workforce. In addition, as the increased subcontractor costs are not reflected in the service hourly rate and overhead recovery is not recouped on sub-contractors this results in an under recovery of full costs from the HRA.

findings.detail: New regulatory requirements for 100% Housing Health and Safety Rating system (HHSRS) stock surveys are generating major cost pressures. The paper explicitly states this reduces the reserve's flexibility to mitigate future HRS fluctuations.
findings.matters: Regulatory compliance costs are forcing the council to underfund capital maintenance reserves, reducing its ability to respond to future stock condition deterioration. This creates a structural squeeze between compliance costs and asset management.

The outcome of these surveys, as anticipated, is forecast to result in increased cost pressures...the HRA has required a reduction in the voluntary contribution to the MRR in order to maintain balances above prudent levels of £1m. Whilst this is a voluntary contribution, it does reduce the flexibility this reserve offers to mitigate any ongoing fluctuations in HRS repairs as the year progresses.
