findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Operational Performance Report - Covering Report - Executive
findings.headline: Complaint response rate fell to 82.3%, missing service standards on 25 of 141 complaints
findings.detail: In Q1 2026/27, the council received 141 complaints. Only 82.3% were responded to within the service standard, with 25 complaints falling outside target response times.
findings.matters: Declining complaint handling performance indicates either resource constraints or process inefficiency, both of which can mask underlying service or financial issues
findings.figures: 82.3% within standard; 25 of 141 outside standard
findings.quote: The percentage of complaints responded to within the service standard decreased this quarter to 82.3% overall. 25 complaints of the 141 responded to in this quarter were outside of the target times.

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Operational Performance Report - Covering Report - Executive
findings.headline: Local Housing Ombudsman found service failure in landlord's handling of resident escalation request in Q1 2026/27
findings.detail: The Local Housing Ombudsman decided one complaint in Q1 2026/27 and found service failure. The landlord failed to recognise a resident's contact as an escalation request, resulting in a delayed stage 2 response.
findings.matters: Ombudsman findings represent formal governance failures and may indicate systemic issues in complaint handling processes or service awareness that could affect other areas
findings.figures: 1 Local Housing Ombudsman complaint decided with finding of service failure
findings.quote: 1 Local Housing Ombudsman (LHO) complaint decided, with a finding of service failure in the landlord's handling of the associated complaint, by failing to recognise the residents contact as an escalation request, thus delaying its stage 2 response.

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Operational Performance Report - Covering Report - Executive
findings.headline: Sickness absence increased 50% year-on-year to 2.51 days per FTE, driven primarily by stress and depression
findings.detail: Sickness levels in Q1 2026/27 reached 2.51 days lost per FTE, up from 1.67 days in Q1 2025/26. The paper identifies stress and depression as the highest cause of both short-term and long-term absence.
findings.matters: Sharp increases in stress-related sickness indicate workforce wellbeing concerns that could affect operational capacity, service delivery, and long-term stability
findings.figures: 2.51 days lost per FTE (Q1 2026/27) vs 1.67 days (Q1 2025/26)
findings.quote: During quarter 1 2026/27 the total sickness levels for the Council stood at 2.51 days lost per FTE. When compared to the same quarter last year sickness levels have also increased (quarter 1 2025/26 figure was 1.67 days lost per FTE). During quarter 1 2026/27, the highest number of days lost due to short term absence was as a result of stress and depression.

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Operational Performance Report - Covering Report - Executive
findings.headline: Staff turnover nearly triples to 3.02% in Q1, up from 1.08% in the previous quarter
findings.detail: The council recorded 20 leavers during Q1 2026/27, representing a turnover rate of 3.02% based on June 2026 headcount. This is a significant increase from the 1.08% turnover in Q4 2025/26, suggesting a sudden change in staffing stability.
findings.matters: Sudden spikes in staff turnover can signal workforce morale problems, management issues, or organisational stress that may affect service continuity and financial control
findings.quote: During quarter 1 2026/27 there were 20 leavers, which equated to a turnover figure of 3.02% (based upon employee headcount at the end of June 2026 excluding apprentices). This figure is higher compared to the previous quarter 4 2025/26 figure of 1.08%.

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Operational Performance Report - Covering Report - Executive
findings.headline: Council housing vacancy losses running at 1.90%, nearly double the 1.00% target
findings.detail: The Housing and Investment Directorate reports that rent loss through dwelling vacancies is currently 1.90%, exceeding the target of 1.00%. The paper attributes this to ongoing operational and compliance-related factors that have persisted from the previous quarter. The council prioritises tenant safety and regulatory compliance before re-letting, which extends vacancy periods.
findings.matters: Housing revenue is a direct income stream for councils; persistent underperformance against target indicates either unmanaged vacancies or structural delays in the re-let process that suppress rental income
findings.figures: 1.90% actual vs 1.00% target
findings.quote: rent loss through dwellings being vacant is currently 1.90%, exceeding the target of 1.00%. Performance during Q1 continues to be affected by several operational and compliance-related factors

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Stewardship and Actual Prudential Indicators Report 2025/26 (Outturn) - Executive Report
findings.headline: Council carrying £41.9m of unfinanced capital expenditure supported by internal cash, depleting reserves to defer borrowing
findings.detail: The Capital Financing Requirement stands at £160.353m but gross borrowing is only £118.489m, creating an under-borrowing position of £41.864m. The report states this gap 'is currently being supported by internal resources'. While this strategy avoids debt service costs on that portion, it exhausts cash reserves that may be needed for operations.
findings.matters: Sustained under-borrowing using internal cash reserves defers the problem rather than solving it; as reserves deplete, the council will eventually have to borrow at higher rates, and meanwhile has reduced flexibility for operational needs.
findings.figures: Capital Financing Requirement £160.353m; gross borrowing £118.489m; under-borrowing gap £41.864m
findings.quote: The Council's total debt (including leases and lease-type arrangements) at 31st March 2026 was £120.501m compared with the Capital Financing Requirement of £160.353m (Appendix A section 3.5). This represents an under-borrowing position of £41,864m, which is currently being supported by internal resources.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Stewardship and Actual Prudential Indicators Report 2025/26 (Outturn) - Executive Report
findings.headline: Investment balances fell 40% to £12.0m, 37% below MTFS forecast, reducing financial flexibility
findings.detail: Total investments fell from £20.083m (2024/25) to £12.028m (2025/26). Average investment balances of £15.43m were significantly below the Medium Term Financial Strategy forecast of £19.2m. This 40% decline in year-end cash reserves reduces the council's buffer to absorb shocks without additional borrowing.
findings.matters: Declining cash reserves compress the council's financial buffer; combined with rising debt service costs and liquidity pressure, they indicate tightening financial capacity.
findings.figures: Total investments £12.028m (2025/26) vs £20.083m (2024/25), down £8.392m; average balances £15.43m vs £19.2m forecast
findings.quote: The Council's Investments at the 31st March 2026 were £11.691m (Appendix A section 4.3), which is £8.392m lower than at 31 st March 2025. Average investment balances for 2025/26 were £15.430m, which was lower than estimated balances of £19.2m in the Medium Term Financial Strategy 2025-30.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Stewardship and Actual Prudential Indicators Report 2025/26 (Outturn) - Executive Report
findings.headline: Liquid reserves dipped below £5m minimum during Q3, requiring emergency short-term borrowing
findings.detail: The council's liquidity benchmark targets £5m minimum liquid short-term deposits. During Q3 'there was a short period where liquid short-term funds dipped slightly below the £5m level; following assessment of the cashflow position short term borrowing was secured to bring liquidity back to normal operating levels'. This represents a near-miss liquidity stress event.
findings.matters: A breach of minimum liquidity levels requiring emergency borrowing signals inadequate cash buffers; the council operates with little headroom against timing shocks.
findings.figures: Minimum liquid deposits target £5m; Q3 actual fell below this threshold requiring short-term borrowing to restore
findings.quote: During Q3 there was a short period where liquid short-term funds dipped slightly below the £5m level; following assessment of the cashflow position short term borrowing was secured to bring liquidity back to normal operating levels.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Stewardship and Actual Prudential Indicators Report 2025/26 (Outturn) - Executive Report
findings.headline: £15.68m of borrowing matures in next 12 months, a nine-fold increase requiring refinancing in a high-rate environment
findings.detail: The maturity profile shows £15.68m (13% of borrowing) due within 12 months, up dramatically from £1.578m the prior year. This creates a material refinancing requirement at elevated rates; MUFG forecasts 5-year PWLB rates between 4.4% and 5.0% through the remainder of 2026.
findings.matters: Large near-term refinancing needs at high rates create cash flow pressure and rollover risk; rates may stay elevated, further increasing debt service costs.
findings.figures: £15.68m due in under 12 months (2025/26) vs £1.578m (2024/25); forecast PWLB 5yr rates 4.4%-5.0% through Mar-27
findings.quote: Under 12 months  15,680 13% 1,578

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Stewardship and Actual Prudential Indicators Report 2025/26 (Outturn) - Executive Report
findings.headline: General Fund financing costs jumped to 15.39% of revenue, a 27% increase driven by higher borrowing and interest rates
findings.detail: Interest payable on General Fund borrowing rose from £1.263m to £1.316m, and financing costs as a percentage of net revenue stream jumped from 12.07% to 15.39%. The council attributes this to refinancing that increased both the volume of debt and the average rate paid, from 3.28% to 3.65%.
findings.matters: A 3.32 percentage point increase in debt service costs signals material deterioration in debt affordability; it reduces revenue available for services and limits flexibility for additional borrowing.
findings.figures: General Fund financing costs 15.39% (2025/26) vs 12.07% (2024/25); average borrowing rate 3.65% vs 3.28%; interest payable £1.316m vs £1.263m
findings.quote: An increase in financing costs across the General Fund as a % of net revenue stream in 2025/26 when compared with 2024/25, is due to refinancing, resulting in the General Fund carrying more debt and more interest paid.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Stewardship and Actual Prudential Indicators Report 2025/26 (Outturn) - Executive Report
findings.headline: Charterholme housing development increased Capital Financing Requirement by £8.4m, dependent on future capital receipts to reduce debt
findings.detail: The General Fund CFR rose from £70.5m to £81.434m, with the increase predominately driven by Charterholme. The council expects to reduce this borrowed amount through 'capital receipts from the sale of the houses' in future years. This represents a material capital commitment whose debt reduction depends on successful completion and sale of housing units.
findings.matters: A large development project with uncertain capital receipts creates credit risk; if house sales underperform, the council carries higher debt longer than anticipated.
findings.figures: General Fund CFR increased from £70.5m to £81.434m; total CFR from £151.946m to £160.353m
findings.quote: The increase in the General Fund CFR is predominately in relation to the Charterholme development, and the upfront cost of the housing delivery. As capital receipts from the sale of the houses are received, these will be applied to the CFR in future years, which will reduce the balance.

findings.headline: Earmarked reserves drawn down by £1.317m to absorb volatility in leisure and business rates income.
findings.detail: Earmarked reserves decreased from £17.643m to £16.326m, a reduction of £1.317m. The most significant movements relate to utilisation of both the Leisure and Business Rates Volatility reserves.
findings.matters: Drawdown of volatility reserves shows the council is experiencing income volatility and using reserves as a buffer; sustained drawdowns could deplete reserves and limit financial flexibility to absorb further shocks.
findings.figures: Earmarked reserves decrease £1.317m (from £17.643m to £16.326m)
findings.quote: The most significant movements in reserves relate to utilisation of both the Leisure and Business Rates Volatility reserves

findings.headline: Total borrowing increased to £118.489m with £15.680m due within 12 months, while interest costs are rising.
findings.detail: Borrowing increased from the prior year, split between short-term borrowing of £15.680m (13%) and long-term borrowing of £102.809m (82%). The average interest rate on borrowing rose to 3.65% from 3.28%, driven by repayment of lower-rate loans.
findings.matters: Material borrowing increase combined with rising interest costs affects debt sustainability and future revenue budget capacity, whilst 13% due within a year creates refinancing pressure.
findings.figures: Total borrowing £118.489m; short-term £15.680m (13%); long-term £102.809m (82%); interest rate 3.65% (up from 3.28%)
findings.quote: Between 31st March 2025 and 31st March 2026, the Council's total borrowing increased to £118.489m (excluding accrued interest which is shown in the Balance Sheet under short-term borrowing as at 31st March 2026)

findings.headline: Current liquidity ratio fallen below 1.0, with the council awaiting better borrowing rates before taking on additional long-term debt.
findings.detail: Current assets (excluding inventories) of £34.879m fall short of current liabilities of £39.235m by a ratio of 0.9:1, down from 1.1:1 the previous year. Management are actively monitoring the liquidity position and deliberately delaying long-term financing until interest rates improve.
findings.matters: A liquidity ratio below 1.0 indicates liquid assets cannot fully cover current liabilities in the short term, raising questions about cash-flow management and the council's flexibility to meet obligations without reserve drawdown or borrowing.
findings.figures: Current assets £34.879m; current liabilities £39.235m; ratio 0.9:1 (prior year 1.1:1)
findings.quote: With the ratio currently below 1.0, management are closely monitoring the Council's liquidity position and are awaiting more favourable long-term borrowing rates before entering into additional long-term financing arrangements

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account running an overspend of £0.245m against budget.
findings.detail: The HRA is reporting a provisional outturn overspend of £0.245m against a budgeted contribution to reserves of £0.112m, generating an overall budget deficit of £0.133m. This contrasts with the General Fund which came in on budget with a £0.03m surplus.
findings.matters: HRA overspends indicate pricing or cost pressures in the council's rental operations, affecting sustainability of housing services and potentially signalling the need for rent increases or reduced investment.
findings.figures: £0.245m overspend; £0.112m budgeted contribution; £0.133m overall deficit; HRA balances £8.481m
findings.quote: The Housing Revenue Account is reporting a provisional outturn overspend of £0.245m against a budgeted contribution to reserves of £0.112m, generating an overall budget deficit of £0.133m

findings.headline: Cornhill Market operating at significant loss in first year with uncertain cost trajectory
findings.detail: The newly opened Cornhill Market incurred £286k net overspend, driven by vacant stalls reducing rental income and additional staffing, maintenance, utility and cleaning costs. The paper notes an update report on first-year operation will be presented in July 2026, but provides no indication of whether costs are settling or whether vacancy levels are expected to improve. This represents an ongoing subsidy requirement for a council-operated facility.
findings.matters: New council operational commitment is not self-sustaining in first year; trajectory for profitability or cost reduction unclear; outcome pending review in July 2026
findings.figures: £286k net overspend in first year; £142k income loss from vacant stalls plus £143k additional operating costs
findings.quote: this predominantly results from a reduction in rental and service charge income due to vacant stalls, plus additional costs primarily relating to staffing, additional maintenance, utility and cleaning contract costs

findings.headline: HRA general balances declining and bad debt provisions rising, signalling tenant arrears management pressures
findings.detail: HRA general balances fell from budgeted £1.295m to actual £1.050m (£245k shortfall). This was driven partly by a £412k increase in bad debt provisions, noted as 'a result of a higher level of current and former tenant arrears write offs in this financial year'. Balances remain within the prudent range of £1-1.5m but the downward trend suggests mounting tenant collection challenges.
findings.matters: Social housing revenue account balances are declining and arrears write-offs are increasing; suggests deterioration in tenant collection; reduces financial buffer against future shocks to HRA income
findings.figures: HRA balances down £245k to £1.050m; bad debt provision increased £412k
findings.quote: The HRA have increased the contribution to the Bad Debt Provision for future years as a result of a higher level of current and former tenant arrears write offs in this financial year

findings.headline: Housing regulatory demands under Awaab's Law driving material increase in repair costs, with escalation expected to continue
findings.detail: Housing Repairs Service experienced £1.218m increase in responsive repairs and void repairs workload due to 'significant increase in repairs works this financial year as a result of regulatory demands from the Regulator of Social Housing'. Sub-contractor costs overran by £904k. The paper states 'The level of work as a result of regulation is expected to continue into next year and beyond'. Funding has been set aside in the MTFS but 'a business case has been drafted and approved by the Executive' is still pending (though the paper says funding is allocated).
findings.matters: Regulatory compliance is driving a structural increase in housing repair costs; the escalation is expected to persist; formal business case for resource allocation still outstanding
findings.figures: £1.218m HRS repair cost increase in 2025/26; sub-contractors overspend £904k
findings.quote: The level of work as a result of regulation is expected to continue into next year and beyond, however funding has been set aside in the latest MTFS, approved at Council in March 2026, to support additional resource once a business case has been drafted and approved by the Executive

findings.headline: Crematorium income falling structurally as market shifts to low-cost direct cremation services elsewhere
findings.detail: Income shortfall of £312k driven by customers switching to competing companies offering direct cremations to crematoria outside Lincoln. The council introduced its own direct cremation option in November 2025 but these new services 'have proved popular' yet remain 'insufficient to meet the overall deficit in income'. A £115k reserve drawdown is being used to offset this ongoing pressure, with the paper noting this needs 'further work' on marketing and service development.
findings.matters: Structural market shift reducing a key council income stream; new service offering does not close the gap; ongoing revenue pressure and reserve depletion required
findings.figures: £312k income deficit; £115k income volatility reserve drawn down
findings.quote: Whilst these have proved popular, and the outturn position is improved from the quarter 3, they are insufficient to meet the overall deficit in income. Work is therefore being considered on how to advertise these new services directly to the public

findings.headline: New leisure centre service contract delivering lower income than bid, requiring ongoing subsidy
findings.detail: The newly reopened leisure centres incurred £673k overspend in 2025/26, with 90% relating to pre-opening and mobilisation costs, plus building repairs and upgrades. The council is now in operational phase and reports a deficit against the original bid. This deficit was offset by drawing down £306k from earmarked reserves set aside for this purpose. The paper states 'this position is expected to improve next year' but provides no evidence or target for breakeven.
findings.matters: A major new contracted service is not delivering to budget and requires ongoing operational subsidy; the improvement pathway is unspecified, creating uncertainty about future annual costs
findings.figures: £673k overspend in 2025/26; £306k reserve drawdown to offset
findings.quote: based on actuals as at the financial year (July-25 to Mar-26) there is a deficit against the original bid, this position is expected to improve next year

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Internal Audit Annual Report - Final
findings.headline: Nine of 16 strategic risks are rated red; five key risks have only limited assurance on management actions
findings.detail: Strategic Risk Register shows 9 red, 6 amber, 1 green. Five strategic risks have limited assurance: protecting council's long-term vision, resilience/capacity to deliver key projects and services, uncertainty around external policies on migration/asylum/prison release, and service delivery.
findings.matters: Multiple red-rated strategic risks with limited assurance over mitigation actions indicate the council faces material uncertainties in its operating environment and ability to respond.
findings.figures: 16 strategic risks: 9 red, 6 amber, 1 green; 5 with limited assurance status
findings.quote: There are currently sixteen Strategic Risks on the register of which nine are red, six amber and one green. All but five have a substantial assurance status. The five with limited assurance status relate to protecting the Councils long term vision, resilience / capacity to deliver key projects and services, uncertainty around external policies on migration, early prison release and asylum dispersal and service delivery.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Internal Audit Annual Report - Final
findings.headline: Performance targets for audit timeliness are consistently unmet; plan completion at 60% against 85-95% target
findings.detail: Audit plan completion is only 60% (target 85-95%), audits completed within 2 months at 53% (target 80%), and draft reports at 82% on time (target 100%). Reasons cited are audit complexity, staff capacity, training time, and management activities.
findings.matters: Slow audit turnaround delays identification of control issues; unmet targets suggest the audit function itself is under-resourced relative to council complexity.
findings.figures: Plan completion 60% vs 85-95% target; audits within 2 months 53% vs 80%; draft reports within 10 days 82% vs 100%
findings.quote: This has not been met due to capacity within the team due to overruns on audits which were more complex than anticipated, additional training time, more time spent on management activities and counter fraud.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Internal Audit Annual Report - Final
findings.headline: Legal services remain red in combined assurance due to capacity and increasing complexity of work
findings.detail: Legal services is flagged as one of six critical activities with low assurance. The issue is specifically capacity and increasing complexity of work. This affects ability to provide timely advice on projects and governance matters.
findings.matters: Without adequate legal support, the council cannot ensure contracts, borrowing decisions, and governance actions are properly reviewed; creates liability and compliance risk.
findings.figures: Legal services identified as red (low assurance); flagged as area where 'financial and legal advice is sought for projects' must be improved
findings.quote: Legal remain the only red in respect of governance as there are still issues with capacity and increasing complexity of work.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Internal Audit Annual Report - Final
findings.headline: Staff capacity remains a key risk, exacerbated by Local Government Reorganisation moving staff away from normal duties
findings.detail: Internal Audit notes that capacity issues have lessened from prior year but remain a key risk. Local Government Reorganisation is now pulling staff time away from normal duties, increasing risk of reduction in control as tasks are rushed or processes shortened. This has been flagged as a risk to monitor in 2026/27 audit planning.
findings.matters: When capacity constraints force process shortcuts, controls break down; with reorganisation ongoing, core service delivery and financial controls could be compromised.
findings.figures: Overruns on audits due to complexity; training time; management activities; counter fraud work all constrained team capacity
findings.quote: Whilst the issues with staff turnover and recruitment have lessened from 2024/25, capacity remains a key risk for the Council. This is increased with the Local Government Reorganisation moving staff time away from normal duties to undertake work required to support the reorganisation.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Internal Audit Annual Report - Final
findings.headline: Three limited assurance audit reports issued; HR-Leavers received limited rating
findings.detail: Two Limited assurance opinions were given in 2025/26, plus a third with indicative Limited rating (same as 2024/25). HR-Leavers audit resulted in Limited assurance with 6 high and 4 medium priority actions. Two follow-up audits from prior Limited reports found actions claimed to be implemented had not been fully implemented.
findings.matters: Limited assurance ratings indicate controls are not operating effectively; HR-Leavers issues could affect payroll accuracy and compliance. False implementation claims suggest inconsistent record-keeping.
findings.figures: 3 Limited assurance reports; HR-Leavers: 6 High, 4 Medium actions; 2024/25 also had 3 Limited reports
findings.quote: During 2025/26 there were two Limited assurance opinions given and there is also a third audit with an indicative assurance level of Limited. This was the same as in 2024/25.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Internal Audit Annual Report - Final
findings.headline: 37 audit actions are overdue as of April 2026, up from previous year, despite implementation rate of only 67%
findings.detail: While age of individual overdue actions has decreased, the total number grew from prior year to 37 by end of April 2026. Overall implementation rate across all 145 agreed actions is 67%. Officers have been required to attend Committee meetings to explain delays.
findings.matters: Rising overdue actions despite revised tracking systems indicate either management capacity problems or resistance to implementing controls; both suggest operational stress.
findings.figures: 37 overdue actions at end of April 2026; 106 total actions agreed (28 High, 78 Medium); 67% overall implementation rate
findings.quote: Whilst the age of the overdue actions has decreased the number has increased this year with there being 37 at the end of April 2026. However the overall implementation rate has increased to 67%.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Internal Audit Annual Report - Final
findings.headline: Debt collection has been a persistent control weakness affecting multiple audit areas
findings.detail: Three separate audit reports have identified debt collection as a significant weakness, with particular issues around collection once debt has passed through the reminder process. Corporate Management Team has been asked to identify root causes and monitor revised processes now in place. This directly impacts council revenue and cash flow.
findings.matters: Weak debt collection reduces council income and indicates operational control failures; a lender would want to see this resolved before it cascades.
findings.figures: Three reports identified debt collection as significant weakness; 37 overdue audit actions at end of April 2026
findings.quote: A common theme has developed over the last two years concerning debt collection. There have been three reports where debt collection was a significant weakness and resulted in a lower assurance rating being given to the areas.

findings.headline: Internal audit identified control gaps in directorate risk registers, with one recommendation not implemented due to resource constraints
findings.detail: The 2024/25 internal audit gave substantial assurance overall but made four recommendations, three medium/low priority. Of these, three were implemented but one was not agreed 'due to the impact on resources'. This indicates the council lacks capacity to implement even low-priority audit recommendations on risk management completeness.
findings.matters: A council unable to resource basic audit recommendations—even on risk register administration—signals stretched finance and operations capacity, increasing the risk that material control gaps emerge undetected.
findings.figures: 4 audit recommendations made: 3 implemented, 1 not implemented due to resource impact
findings.quote: Of the four recommendations made, three were implemented with the fourth (green) recommendation not agreed for implementation due to the impact on resources.

findings.headline: Government policy on migration, asylum and early prison release poses a High risk to service delivery, capacity and the MTFS
findings.detail: Risk #14 specifically identifies impacts from uncertainty around government policies on migration dispersal, asylum, and early prison release as creating High risk (Probable likelihood, Critical impact) to the council's service delivery, capacity and MTFS. The paper explicitly links this to impacts on housing, communities and city centre economic vitality.
findings.matters: External policy-driven service demand that the council cannot control but must fund poses a material risk to financial stability. If central government policy shifts increase service demand without proportional funding, it creates unplanned pressure on the MTFS.
findings.figures: Risk #14: High rating, Probable likelihood, Critical impact
findings.quote: Impacts of the uncertainty of Government's policies on migration policy, asylum dispersal, early prison release etc on the Council's service delivery, capacity and MTFS as well as the impacts on housing, communities and the economic vitality of the City Centre.

findings.headline: General Fund MTFS rated High risk with Probable likelihood and Critical impact
findings.detail: Risk #2 in the Strategic Risk Register is rated High with Probable likelihood and Critical impact, specifically concerning the General Fund MTFS. This represents the council's core financial planning risk and suggests material concern about the sustainability of current spending and revenue plans.
findings.matters: A High-rated MTFS risk is the clearest signal that the council's finance director cannot confidently plan beyond the immediate term, which is material to any lending decision.
findings.figures: Risk #2: High rating, Probable likelihood, Critical impact
findings.quote: Failure to deliver a sustainable Medium-Term Financial Strategy that supports delivery of the Council's Vision (specifically in relation to the General Fund).

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement Report - Audit Committee 2026
findings.headline: Directorates not consistently seeking financial and legal advice on projects in a timely manner
findings.detail: The council identifies an ongoing need for all directorates to improve their practice of seeking timely financial and legal advice, indicating this has been a recurring pattern requiring monitoring.
findings.matters: Projects proceeding without timely professional review increases the risk of financial error, legal non-compliance, or reputational loss requiring later remediation.
findings.figures: all directorates
findings.quote: There is an ongoing need for all directorates to ensure financial and legal advice is sought for projects in a timely manner.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement Report - Audit Committee 2026
findings.headline: Limited professional capacity constrains governance of complex projects amid Local Government Reorganisation
findings.detail: The council explicitly states it lacks sufficient internal professional support capacity to provide advice and oversight for significant and complex projects, compounded by Vision 2030 delivery and the organisational impact of pending Local Government Reorganisation.
findings.matters: Insufficient professional capacity during a major reorganisation creates risk that large projects lack adequate financial, legal, or technical oversight, leading to delays, cost overruns, or delivery failure.
findings.figures: Vision 2030; Local Government Re-organisation
findings.quote: There remains limited additional capacity within internal professional support services to provide the advice and oversight necessary to ensure effective governance of significant and complex projects ensuring delivery of Vision 2030, maintaining business as usual alongside the impact on services with the additional requirement of Local Government Re-organisation.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement Report - Audit Committee 2026
findings.headline: Debt management across all service areas identified as a governance issue requiring Corporate Management Team oversight
findings.detail: The council has identified debt management across the entire council as a governance weakness that requires actions to be completed and ongoing oversight by CMT during 2026/27.
findings.matters: Council-wide debt management issues suggest either collection failures, overspend recovery problems, or lack of control over service area spending—all material to cash position and service cost.
findings.figures: all service areas
findings.quote: Debt management over all service areas which actions will need completing and oversight by CMT over the coming year

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement Report - Audit Committee 2026
findings.headline: Internal Audit has issued three limited assurance reports for Markets, Leavers and Housing Rents
findings.detail: These three service areas have failed internal audit review and are flagged for monitoring in 2026/27. Limited assurance means controls are not working as designed and present a higher risk of error or loss.
findings.matters: Limited assurance audit findings indicate material control weaknesses that could affect service delivery, financial accuracy, or asset protection in specific revenue-generating areas.
findings.figures: three limited assurance reports
findings.quote: Internal Audit has issued three limited assurance reports for Markets, Leavers and Housing Rents which will require monitoring over the year

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 - FINAL
findings.headline: Council maintains £39m under-borrowed position, betting interest rates will fall
findings.detail: The council deliberately does not borrow its full capital need (CFR), instead using reserves. Under-borrowing position is £38.9m (2026/27). Strategy justifies this by stating medium/long rates 'are forecast to fall' and plans to 'adopt a pragmatic approach to changing circumstances.' If rates don't fall as forecast, the council risks locking in higher costs or depleting reserves faster than planned.
findings.matters: Under-borrowing is a timing strategy. If interest rate forecasts prove wrong or economic conditions shift, the council may be forced to borrow at higher rates later or to draw reserves further, reducing financial flexibility and increasing refinancing risk.
findings.figures: Under-borrowing 2026/27: £38,933k. CFR 2026/27: £157,327k. External borrowing 2026/27: £118,395k.
findings.quote: The Council is currently maintaining an under-borrowed position. This means that the capital borrowing need (the CFR), has not been fully funded with loan debt as cash supporting the Council's reserves, balances and cash flow has been used as a temporary measure.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 - FINAL
findings.headline: Core financial reserves thin 23% by 2026/27 to £42.45m, Major Repairs Reserve halved
findings.detail: Total core funds forecast to fall from £54.73m (2024/25 actual) to £42.45m (2026/27 estimate), a 23% reduction. Major Repairs Reserve depletes 51% from £22.98m to £11.30m to fund HRA capital. Recovery is projected thereafter, but the interim thinning reduces financial resilience.
findings.matters: Reserves cushion service shocks and unplanned costs. A 23% reduction in one cycle, plus 51% MRR depletion to fund housing works, signals the council is running leaner and leaves less room for error if income shortfalls or overspends occur.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 - FINAL
findings.headline: HRA financing costs rise to 30.64% in 2026/27 and 30.90% in 2027/28 as new build program intensifies
findings.detail: Housing Revenue Account financing costs climb from 28.67% (2025/26) to 30.64% (2026/27) and peak at 30.90% (2027/28), driven by HRA capital investment of £27m+ annually. This high ratio leaves little headroom if rental income falters or costs overshoot.
findings.matters: The HRA is ring-fenced and self-financing. If financing costs exceed 30%, repairs and maintenance could be deferred if rental income does not grow proportionally, eroding asset condition and future revenue.
findings.quote: HRA (including New Build) 28.67% 30.64% 30.90% 30.44%

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 - FINAL
findings.headline: General Fund capital spending drops 77% from £28.24m (2025/26) to £6.57m (2026/27), then falls to £1.3m annually
findings.detail: General Fund capital expenditure drops from £28,240k in 2025/26 to £6,574k in 2026/27, then remains minimal at £1.3m annually. The strategy presents these numbers without explaining the cause—whether it reflects completed programs or budget-driven cuts that may continue.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether capital investment halts permanently or temporarily. Sustained low capital spending can indicate deferred maintenance, budget constraints, or reduced service capacity.
findings.figures: General Fund capital: 2025/26 £28,240k; 2026/27 £6,574k (77% reduction). Following years: £1,307k and £1,316k.

findings.headline: Council must ensure capital commitments do not create legacy financial issues for new unitary authority
findings.detail: The paper explicitly requires the Council to consider long-term revenue implications of capital expenditure when evaluating projects, to avoid imposing financial burdens on the new unitary authority. This is a government mandate within the reorganisation framework and creates a constraint on capital investment decisions.
findings.matters: Government has signalled that councils making unsustainable commitments during transition period may face intervention; this constrains the Council's ability to make aggressive capital investments even where funding is available.
findings.figures: Capital programmes 2026-31: £11.710m (GIP) and £86.887m (HIP)
findings.quote: In allocating capital resources and committing to new capital investments the Council will therefore need to be cognisant of the implications this may create for a new unitary authority and ensure it does not create any additional legacy issues.

findings.headline: Local government reorganisation will create significant organisational capacity strain during capital delivery period
findings.detail: The transition to a single-tier unitary authority (abolishing the current two-tier shire system) will demand 'extraordinary focus, planning and resource management' from the Council. This transition runs concurrent with delivery of Vision 2030 capital priorities. The Council explicitly recognises this will require a balance of capacity and may impact delivery of planned capital schemes.
findings.matters: Organisational distraction during a major capital investment period creates delivery risk; capital schemes may slip or be deprioritised as management attention is drawn to the LGR integration process.
findings.figures: Reorganisation planned; Vision 2030 delivery period overlaps with LGR transition
findings.quote: The transition to a new unitary authority will demand extraordinary focus, planning and resource management by the Council and will inevitably require a balance of capacity between this, delivery of Vision 2030 and maintaining full service delivery. This may impact on the delivery on some of the planned capital schemes as part of Vision 2030.

findings.headline: HRA borrowing increasing to £87.6m to fund new build and existing stock investment
findings.detail: Housing Revenue Account debt is rising from current £81.4m to £87.6m by the end of the MTFS period (2031). This additional £6.2m borrowing is being used to fund new build housing and purchase-and-repair expenditure. HRA borrowing costs are currently 6.79% of gross HRA revenue expenditure, trending upward to 7.06% in 2027/28.
findings.matters: For a lender, rising HRA debt levels and borrowing costs indicate increased service dependency on sustained rental income; HRA vulnerability to policy changes (e.g. rent controls) has direct impact on repayment capacity.
findings.figures: HRA borrowing: £81.4m (current) to £87.6m (end of MTFS); HRA borrowing cost 2026/27: 6.79% of gross expenditure; 2027/28: 7.06%; limit: 14%
findings.quote: Currently the HRA borrowing requirement stands at £81.4m and is expected to increase to £87.6m by the end of the MTFS period. This additional borrowing is being used to fund new build and purchase & repair expenditure.

findings.headline: National planning policy now requires Lincoln to deliver 40% more housing annually
findings.detail: New mandatory housing targets issued December 2024 increased Central Lincolnshire's annual delivery requirement from 1,102 to 1,552 dwellings per year. Lincoln's share rose to 413 per year, with a 5% buffer bringing the planning requirement to 1,630 per year. From July 2026, an additional 20% buffer applies for five-year land supply calculations.
findings.matters: This represents a material acceleration in housing delivery expectations within the Council's capital programme period; failure to meet targets creates planning risk and may trigger intervention from government.
findings.figures: Housing target increase: 40% (from 1,102 to 1,552 per annum for partnership); Lincoln's allocation: 413 per year; with 5% buffer: 1,630 per year; transitional 20% buffer applies from 1 July 2026
findings.quote: For the Central Lincolnshire Partnership, which consists of Lincoln, West Lindsey District Council and North Kesteven District Council the housing targets have increased by 40% from 1,102 to 1,552, allocated as: Lincoln 413; West Lindsey 487 and North Kesteven 652 per year. In addition to this, the NPPF also requires an additional 5% buffer to be applied, brought forward from later in the plan period, resulting in a need to plan for and deliver 1,630 dwellings per year.

findings.headline: General Fund capital programme is dependent on property sales from a single development
findings.detail: The Council's ability to fund General Fund capital investment is currently reliant on capital receipts from Phase 1a property sales at the Charterholme development. If these sales do not materialise as planned, there is no identified alternative funding source for the general investment programme.
findings.matters: Single-point dependency for funding a £11.7m five-year programme represents material delivery risk; any delay or failure in this development phase would immediately constrain council's capital investment capability.
findings.figures: General Investment Programme budget 2026-31: £11.710m; Phase 1a to deliver first 52 market homes
findings.quote: Currently the level of capital resources required to fund the capital programme in the General Fund is reliant upon property disposals from Phase 1a of the Charterholme development.

findings.headline: Mayoral Combined Authority may redirect external funding away from the Council
findings.detail: Lincoln's external funding streams, including Homes England and Affordable Homes Programme grants currently allocated directly to the Council, are likely to be channelled through the new Greater Lincolnshire Mayoral Combined Authority instead. These will be allocated according to the MCA's priorities, not the Council's. The paper explicitly states this creates risk for capital project delivery.
findings.matters: The Council relies heavily on external grants to deliver capital priorities. Loss of direct access to major funding streams would materially constrain capital delivery capability.
findings.figures: Council's capital programmes are £11.710m (GIP) and £86.887m (HIP) for 2026-31; reliance on external funding is 'high' according to the strategy
findings.quote: with the creation of the MCA there is a high likelihood that funding will instead be channelled through it, and will be subject to allocation in line with its priorities. This creates a risk that the Council will no longer be able to access funding opportunities and ensure they are used in accordance with the needs of the City, it's residents and businesses and could also limit funding to take forward key capital projects in support of Vision 2030. Given the reliance on external funding to deliver capital projects this would only create further funding pressures.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-2031 FINAL
findings.headline: Council establishing Future Readiness/Transition reserve for LGR costs with quantum and composition undefined.
findings.detail: The council is setting aside resources in a dedicated Future Readiness/Transition reserve to fund its share of upfront reorganisation costs and its own internal transition costs ahead of the 2028 merger. The council acknowledges 'it is prudent to set resources aside to fund those costs when they occur' but the total cost, the council's share, and the composition of the reserve are not yet known.
findings.matters: A material but unquantified cost is being deferred. Until the reorganisation costs are known, the council cannot accurately forecast reserve adequacy or the true cost of the transition. This creates forecasting uncertainty for the 2027/28 and 2028/29 budgets.
findings.figures: Amount and composition of Future Readiness/Transition reserve: TBD
findings.quote: While neither the total cost nor the Council's share of these upfront reorganisation costs are yet known with certainty, it is prudent to set resources aside to fund those costs when the occur. The Council has therefore established a Future Readiness/Transition reserve

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-2031 FINAL
findings.headline: Central Lincolnshire housing target increases 40% to 1,552 dwellings per year, with Lincoln required to deliver 413 per year.
findings.detail: The new National Planning Policy Framework increases the Central Lincolnshire Partnership housing target by 40% from 1,102 to 1,552 per year. Lincoln's allocation is 413 per year. With a mandatory 5% buffer, the effective target is 1,630 per year across the partnership. Transitional arrangements add a further 20% buffer until April 2028, when the full requirement takes effect.
findings.matters: Failure to deliver against housing targets triggers planning enforcement; success requires capital investment and effective master-planning. For a small city council, a 40% increase in annual housing delivery is material to capital planning, infrastructure pressure, and service demand forecasts.
findings.figures: 1,102 to 1,552 dwellings per year (40% increase); Lincoln 413 per year; 1,630 with 5% buffer; transitional 20% buffer until April 2028
findings.quote: For the Central Lincolnshire Partnership, which consists of Lincoln, West Lindsey District Council and North Kesteven District Council the housing targets have increased by 40% from 1,102 to 1,552, allocated as: Lincoln 413

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-2031 FINAL
findings.headline: Fair Funding Review closes structural budget deficit with £2.28m (28.6%) funding increase, but reveals 15 years of systematic underfunding.
findings.detail: The FFR 2.0 outcome means the council no longer needs the £1.75m annual savings target that the previous MTFS was built on. The 28.6% increase in the Fair Funding Allocation by 2028/29 closed the structural gap between income and expenditure. However, this increase reveals the council was systematically underfunded since 2011 under the old system. Over the last decade, the council delivered £10.5m in annual revenue savings to manage the budget gap while protecting core services.
findings.matters: While near-term funding improves, the decade of austerity-driven savings has already constrained the council's capacity. The FFR benefit is real but relatively short-lived given the 2028 LGR date. Lenders should understand the council was operating under structural stress for 15 years.
findings.figures: £2.280m (28.6%) increase in FFA by 2028/29; £10.5m in annual revenue savings delivered over last decade; £1.75m annual savings target (now negated)
findings.quote: The 2028/29 Fair Funding Allocation (FFA), after removal of all transitional arrangements, announced in the Finance Settlement is £2.280m higher (28.6%) than the 2025/26 baseline... During the last decade the Council has delivered annual revenue savings of over £10.5m

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-2031 FINAL
findings.headline: Council terminates 31 March 2028 under Local Government Reorganisation, with material and unquantified transition costs.
findings.detail: Government has set a firm date for LGR: the City of Lincoln Council in its current structure will cease to exist and merge into a new unitary authority on 1 April 2028. The council is establishing a Future Readiness/Transition reserve to fund its share of upfront reorganisation costs and internal transition costs, but the amount is not yet known. This creates a 2-part financial strategy with different treatment of resources before and after 2028.
findings.matters: Lenders need certainty about borrowing repayment capacity; a terminal date of 15 months from the MTFS publish date creates fundamental questions about legacy liabilities and asset stranding. Transition costs will draw down reserves.
findings.figures: 31 March 2028 terminal date; upfront reorganisation costs unknown; reserve established but amount TBD
findings.quote: Under the Government's current timetable for LGR, the City of Lincoln Council, in it's current structure, would cease to exist beyond 31 st March 2028.

findings.headline: Charterholme Housing Development borrowing will be repaid from capital receipts with no Minimum Revenue Provision allocated
findings.detail: The council has made no MRP provision for borrowing related to Charterholme Housing Development, stating that any borrowing will be short-term and repaid using capital receipts within the MTFS period.
findings.matters: If the projected capital receipts do not materialise, the council may face an unexpected funding gap for debt repayment. This is material given April 2024 regulatory changes that explicitly prohibited use of capital receipts as replacement for revenue charges.
findings.figures: None provided for scheme size
findings.quote: There has been no Minimum Revenue Provision made within the MTFS relating to the Charterholme Housing Development as this element of the scheme relates to housing provision, and any borrowing related to this scheme will be short term and repaid using capital receipts, within the period of the MTFS.

findings.headline: Capital expenditure is forecast to decline 34% in 2026/27 and a further 38% in 2027/28
findings.detail: Total capital spending falls from £51.4m (2025/26) to £33.7m (2026/27) to £20.9m (2027/28). General Fund capital expenditure shows the sharpest drop, falling from £28.2m to £6.6m to £1.3m across the forecast period.
findings.matters: A sharp and sustained reduction in capital investment signals either financial constraint, service reductions, or deferral of maintenance and development; a lender would want to understand which.
findings.quote: Capital Expenditure General Fund 28,240 / 6,574 / 1,307 / 1,316 and HRA 23,161 / 27,088 / 19,572 / 13,568

findings.headline: Operational and Authorised Limits for borrowing have been recalculated upward by 37–38% following a methodology review
findings.detail: The Operational Boundary increased from £121.5m to £168.5m and the Authorised Limit from £128.9m to £177.5m. The council states this reflects a methodology change and that no limits have been breached, with no change to the underlying Capital Financing Requirement.
findings.matters: A lender would want to understand what prompted this significant recalibration, whether it signals expansion of future borrowing capacity, and how the council arrived at the new methodology.
findings.quote: During the year, a review of the methodology around the calculation of both the Operational Boundary and Authorised limits has been conducted. Whilst the outcome of the review has seen a significant increase to both limits, there is no change to the Council's CFR (other than decisions taken by Executive) and no limits have been breached at any point.

findings.headline: Charterholme Development borrowing will be short-term, repaid from capital receipts, and excluded from debt repayment (MRP) calculations.
findings.detail: The council has excluded the Charterholme Development from Minimum Revenue Provision, indicating borrowing related to this housing and regeneration scheme is short-term and will be repaid using capital receipts within the forecasted period. This special treatment differs from normal capital projects.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand how major capital schemes are financed, particularly when short-term borrowing relies on achieving capital receipts targets to repay the debt.
findings.figures: No amounts specified for the Charterholme Development.
findings.quote: There has been no Minimum Revenue Provision made within the MTFS relating to the Charterholme Development as the scheme relates to housing provision/regeneration and any borrowing related to this scheme will be short term and repaid using capital receipts, within the period of the MTFS

findings.paper_title: Report by Jane Nellist, Independent Chair of the Audit Committee
findings.headline: Limited assurance identified on Fleet management
findings.detail: The 2024-25 internal audit identified limited assurance on Fleet management, meaning controls require improvement and the activity is unlikely to fully meet its objectives.
findings.matters: Effective asset and fleet management affects operational efficiency and value for money; limited assurance indicates control weaknesses that could impact service delivery.
findings.figures: Limited assurance report; one of two limited assurance reports issued during 2024/25
findings.quote: The two limited assurance reports issued during 2024/25 were Fleet and Debtors/recovery.

findings.paper_title: Report by Jane Nellist, Independent Chair of the Audit Committee
findings.headline: Cyber fraud identified as Red risk in strategic risk register
findings.detail: Cyber fraud is flagged as a Red (highest risk level) within the council's Strategic Risk register. The council states it continues to place high importance on cyber security due to ongoing cyber threats.
findings.matters: A Red-rated strategic risk indicates a material threat to the council's operations, data security, and financial systems that requires ongoing senior management attention and resources.
findings.figures: Red risk rating in Strategic Risk register
findings.quote: The cyber fraud threat is an ongoing risk and the Council continues to place high importance on cyber security and has included it as an Amber risk (combined with other IT related risks) within the Fraud Risk Register and a Red risk in the Strategic Risk register.

findings.paper_title: Report by Jane Nellist, Independent Chair of the Audit Committee
findings.headline: External auditor KPMG identified two amber-rated recommendations on internal controls
findings.detail: KPMG issued two priority-2 (amber) recommendations following their 2024-25 audit, relating to internal controls relevant to the preparation of financial statements. These represent specific areas where the control framework requires improvement.
findings.matters: Audit recommendations on financial statement controls indicate weaknesses in governance and accounting procedures that affect the reliability of financial reporting.
findings.figures: Two priority two (amber) recommendations from external auditor
findings.quote: As part of the audit work undertaken, KPMG considered the internal controls in place to be relevant to the preparation of the financial statements. The findings of this work resulted in two, priority two (amber) recommendations being made.

findings.paper_title: Report by Jane Nellist, Independent Chair of the Audit Committee
findings.headline: Internal control environment rated amber due to resource capacity constraints
findings.detail: The 2024-25 Annual Internal Audit Report gave 'Performing Adequately' (amber) assurance for internal control. This amber rating was specifically attributed to resource capacity issues within the audit function, which can impact the effectiveness of monitoring the control environment.
findings.matters: Resource constraints in internal audit suggest the council's control environment may not be as rigorously monitored as required, increasing the risk that issues could go undetected.
findings.figures: Amber assurance rating for internal control; audit team comprises three staff members
findings.quote: In terms of internal control, this level of assurance was due to a number of factors including two limited assurance reports and resource capacity, which can have an impact on the internal control environment.

findings.headline: Internal audit issued limited assurance on Debtors/Recovery function
findings.detail: The 2024-25 internal audit identified limited assurance on Debtors/Recovery. Limited assurance means controls in place require improvement and it is unlikely that the activity will fully meet its objectives.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence in the council's ability to collect money owed; limited assurance indicates a control weakness that could affect cash flow and financial stability.
findings.figures: Limited assurance report; one of two limited assurance reports issued during 2024/25
findings.quote: The two limited assurance reports issued during 2024/25 were Fleet and Debtors/recovery.

findings.headline: External audit identified two areas requiring internal control recommendations.
findings.detail: During the audit, KPMG made two recommendations around internal controls. Management has provided comment on these recommendations, and further details are contained in page 28 of the full KPMG report.
findings.matters: Internal control weaknesses are of direct concern to lenders as they affect the council's ability to produce accurate and reliable financial information.
findings.figures: Two control recommendations
findings.quote: two recommendations were made around internal controls that management have made comment on

findings.detail: The external audit found three misstatements above the £100,000 threshold in the draft financial statements. All three errors were identified and corrected in the final version of the accounts before publication. The detailed breakdown is provided in the full KPMG report (page 27).
findings.matters: Material errors in financial statements suggest underlying weaknesses in the council's financial reporting controls or procedures, which affects the reliability of accounts.
findings.figures: Three misstatements above £100k threshold

news_drafts.headline: Lincoln council housing account closes 2025/26 with £8.481m balance, from £8.913m a year earlier
news_drafts.lead:
City of Lincoln Council's housing revenue account, the ring-fenced account for its own housing stock, paid for by rents, carried forward a balance of £8.481m at 31 March 2026. The balance brought forward at the start of the year was £8.913m. The figures are in the summary accounts for 2025, which are Appendix A to the papers for the Audit Committee meeting of 16 November 2026.

The account shows income of £38.016m and spending of £24.939m for the year, which leaves a net cost of service of £(13.078)m, a positive result before financing. After financing, the council made an appropriation of £11.503m to the Major Repairs Reserve, a reserve set aside for repairs to the housing stock. It also made a transfer of £300k to housing revenue account reserves.

The paper records a surplus of £133k for the year. The balance carried forward appears in the accounts as "HRA balance carried forward 8,481", in thousands of pounds.
